posts.copy:
Costco stocks almost a tenth of the products a Korean hypermarket does. Not by accident, but by design.

A typical Costco store carries about 4,000 types of item. Korean big-box stores carry close to ten times that.

In its 2024 financial year, Costco Korea's average sales per store were 343.6 billion won. That is four to five times what a Korean big-box store does.

In the year to August 2025 its revenue reached 7.32 trillion won, up 12.1%, from 20 stores. That took it past Homeplus, the No. 2 hypermarket chain, on 6.99 trillion won.

The unlock was pricing architecture, not localisation.

It did not widen the range to match local rivals. It did not lift its margins to local levels either. It targets a 15.1% margin per product, against 26.9% at E-Mart. The membership fee does the rest.

The instinct when entering a new Asian market is to add. Local ranges, local promotions, local everything, until the entrant is a more expensive copy of the incumbent.

Sometimes the model is the product. The job is knowing which parts must change for a market, and which must not.

We have never worked with Costco. This is commentary from the outside.

If you want your APAC go-to-market to look like this, work with us.

Source: KED Global, 19 November 2024; The Korea Herald, 20 November 2025

posts.copy:
Asics' lifestyle sneakers grew 77% in Europe in the first half of 2026. Its running shoes grew 10%.

Same company. A lot of the same shoes. A different buyer.

The product was never the problem. Performance running grew in every region Asics sells in.

What changed was who it is for. A runner buys on cushioning and mileage. The SportStyle buyer buys on the archive, the colourway, and who else is wearing it.

So Asics rebuilt the other two things.

The price. Its own filing says the range is "shifting toward a more premium direction, with a focus on products priced above USD100."

The story. Models from the '90s and '00s, restructured as archive lines, and collaborations with designers such as Kiko Kostadinov.

Across Europe, sales were up 29.7% on a currency-neutral basis, with SportStyle leading.

This is the pattern in most Asia-to-West moves we see. The product rarely needs to change. The buyer is a different person, the price has to be rebuilt for how they buy, and the story has to be written for them.

Rebuilding those three is what our GTM advisory work is for.

We have never worked with Asics. This is commentary from the outside.

If you want your move into the West to look like this, work with us.

posts.copy:
Companies say they want a real business in APAC, then hand the whole region to one new hire with a laptop and a global target.

We start with four things:

→ First market
→ Mandate
→ Target
→ Back-up

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Did your hire choose the first market, or inherit a list of six from a slide at head office?

Is their target built from what this market buys, or from your home-market conversion rates?

Can they set price and sign a partner, or does every discount need a late-night call to head office?

When a distributor goes quiet, who do they call? Someone who knows the market, or someone who knows the product?

From the inside this looks like a hiring problem. The numbers are slow, so the answer must be a better country manager. Sometimes it is. More often the job was set up so that nobody could do it, and the next hire inherits the same job.

APAC is not one market. It is 15+ ecosystems with different rules, cultures and buyer behaviour, and nobody recalibrates fifteen of them alone.

A first conversation usually tells us whether we are useful to you. Sometimes the answer is no.

If you are a year into your first APAC hire and the pipeline still has not moved, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures
